I am about to complete my first year of a masters in bioinformatics. This past year we have extensive DBMS, R, Python, Shell, Java, functional programming, Dynamical Systems, Linear Models, and protein model building. Next semester we have machine learning, evolutionary biology, genomics, Bayesian mathematics, and multivariate statistics. Then we have our thesis semester with a support vector machine course. My linear algebra is a little weak so I will brush up this summer, but other than that is there anything I should try and learn for after my MSc.
Any recommendations on what I should brush up on?
That's an exciting courseload, what are your professional interests? What subfields do you plan on working in? A little information like that would help us see what else you might want to look into.

Yeah my program really focuses on the theory. They taught us programming and bare bones tools and basically said every job is different, now you know enough to teach yourself. The think bioinformatics is changing too fast to teach any specific tools or analysis. So we learn a lot of math/engineering to able understand how all of the tools work and to write our own if need be.

My field or my thesis rather will be in space biology. I am hoping to continue as a PhD as well. Now I know that's really niche so let's just say it is mostly whole genome gene expression. We also had an extensive data visualization course, I am super interested in that.

Could I ask what program that is? It sounds very well executed, sounds like a great program. But to your question ... you say DBMS, which makes me think that that is a generalized education (which is a great idea on the school's part) but you would benefit from learning or brushing up on specific database tools like MySQL, for instance. Also, you're taking courses on Dynamics. Stochastics, Bernoulli/Poisson processes etc. can play a large role in molecular dynamics/proteomics.

By and large, I think the best strategy is to familiarize yourself with core principals, which your program is doing for you; R, Database, a flexible language, Non-Linear Dynamics, Statistics, Linear Algebra and numerical analysis, and then begin to move closer to your astrobiology (of which, I really know nothing). I believe /u/Fordrus works much more in genomics than I do, hopefully s/he will be able to provide some more advice.

Also, something that I like to do is that while I'm perusing the internet and I come across a particularly interesting research group or project, a lot of times they will be hosted on websites that provide tons of educational material. University Illinois Champaign, for instance (and like many other programs), develops its own software and supplies loads of up to date tutorials and real world problems to try out.. So if you want to scratch some itch that you have to work on astrobiology, find a research group and read their documentation. It's not always on their websites, though. CERN developed the scientific Linux Distro with EPFL et al. which was pretty successful, but you have to go looking for it.

I had edited my post but it didn't stick. We have talk two intensive DB courses. One that is general that taught us theory and mysql and one that geared towards bioinformatics which taught us about the DBS used in bioinformatics and their tools (mongoDB, neo4j, hadoop, sqllite) both were great courses.

The course is the MSc./MEg./Master of bioengineering(depends on your bachelors which degree they give) of Bioinformatics in KU Leuven in Belgium. It is really and amazing well developed program.

I think a course-centric perspective is the wrong way to approach your question. Rather, try to develop a perspective from what's happening in the field. Your program seems to be strong on the theory, now go through Science, Nature, Cell ... read an article - almost all have significant bioinformatics components these days. Do you understand the biology? Do you understand it deep enough to critique it, to improve on the question? What additional computational experiments could you do to explore interesting new avenues that arise from what's been published? How can you improve on their methodology? That's the kind of thinking you need to develop. Work from a project-centric perspective and develop your own interests. Then, if you need more background, you can consider additional contents-learning. But it is rather likely that course-based work is not going to be optimal, the information half-life in the field is just too short these days.
